title: Chart Spin — the same numbers, both ways
subtitle: One query, two opposite arguments — plus four more ways a technically correct chart misleads: raw counts, rank encoding, the wrong form, and axis order

source.publisher: Same DOHMH data as the Inspections tab — that is the point
source.note: Both charts below are produced by one script in one run from one API call. No data was added, removed, or altered between them. Everything that differs is a display choice.

grain.row_is: one violation citation, rated per inspection
grain.note: The honest chart's window was fixed by the question before looking. The spun chart's window was chosen by searching all 15 possible 12-month starts for the one that maximized Brooklyn's slope — a choice that leaves no visual trace whatsoever. The last two charts widen the lesson past framing into form itself — a denominator that ranks population, a rank encoding that hides magnitude, and a map for a pattern with no geography.

charts.title: The honest render
charts.insight: Brooklyn's violations-per-inspection went 3.67 → 3.67 over the last twelve complete months. Flat. Its annualized drift (+0.19/yr) ranks third behind the Bronx (+0.32) and Manhattan (+0.23), and all five boroughs sit inside a narrow band.
charts.form: Multi-line, zero baseline, one accented series
charts.form_why: The claim under test was about change over time across groups, so time goes on x and every borough shares one y-scale. Graying four series and accenting one is emphasis — it directs attention without altering what any line shows.
charts.method: y-axis from zero so visible change equals real change. Window = last 12 complete calendar months, fixed by the question before any data was seen. No smoothing. Identical treatment for every line. Partial current month excluded.
charts.caution: This chart's headline is that a premise handed to us — 'Brooklyn is steadily rising while others stay flat' — turned out to be false. The honest render could not make that claim, so it doesn't.

charts.title: The spun render — same data, four levers moved
charts.insight: 'BROOKLYN VIOLATIONS SURGE 12 MONTHS RUNNING.' Manufactured from a 14% wobble in a dataset where the honest answer was +0.00. Nothing here is fabricated; every plotted value is real.
charts.form_why: Identical form, opposite conclusion — which is the whole demonstration. Spin does not require a different chart type or a false number. It requires four defensible-sounding choices.
charts.method: 1) Window cherry-picked as the max-slope option out of 15 candidates, starting at Brooklyn's trough. 2) y-axis zoomed to Brooklyn's own range, so a 14% change fills 100% of panel height — hiding behind the true rule that line charts need not start at zero. 3) Tall-narrow aspect ratio amplifies any slope; nobody audits aspect ratio. 4) Three-month smoothing applied to Brooklyn ONLY (disclosed at 5.5pt), so its cleaned line reads as signal while the raw grays read as noise.
charts.caution: Every individual choice here has a legitimate use, and each could be defended in a meeting by citing a real principle. That is what makes this the realistic failure mode — far more common than fabricated data, and much harder to catch.

charts.title: Watch it happen — the honest chart becomes the spun one, one lever at a time
charts.insight: The two renders above are separated by six display decisions and nothing else. This piece pins one chart to your screen and fires the levers in sequence as you scroll — baseline, window, aspect, smoothing, color, title. Brooklyn is 3.67 → 3.67 the entire time, and the final step reverses everything at once to prove it.
charts.form: Scrollytelling — a pinned chart the reader transforms by scrolling
charts.form_why: A gallery can only assert that the honest and spun charts are the same data; a scroll piece demonstrates it, because the reader watches the transformation happen and can scroll back to any point. The pattern and the trigger library (scrollama.js, MIT) come from The Pudding, who open-source the machinery behind their visual essays.
charts.method: The chart renders client-side from borough-series.json — the same numbers the PNGs were drawn from, exported by the same guarded pull under the same watermark. Six of this tab's seven levers fire one per step; encoding, the seventh, is covered by the map and bump-chart exhibits below. Falls back to the static side-by-side when JavaScript is off.
charts.caution: Sequencing is itself a display choice. Showing the levers one at a time argues they are separable, when in a real spun chart they arrive together and reinforce each other — the piece says so on the page rather than leaving it implicit.

charts.title: Side by side — every axis labeled, and the right panel still lies
charts.insight: Both panels carry full axis labels and their own disclosure line. The deception survives anyway, because it lives in the frame rather than in anything a label can name.
charts.form_why: Equal panels isolate the levers under study. An earlier version drew the spun panel narrower — preserving the aspect trick — which confounded 'the y-axis is zoomed' with 'the panel is squished' and made the comparison itself guilty of the thing it teaches.
charts.method: Left and right render from the same array of numbers in the same script execution. The only differences are y-range, window, and which series got smoothed.
charts.caution: 'The axes are labeled, just read them' is the standard defense of a spun chart. This image is the counterexample. Window, y-range, aspect ratio and asymmetric smoothing have no axis labels — so a reader who checks only the labels has audited nothing.

charts.title: Raw counts rank by size — and rank encoding hides how small the gap is
charts.insight: A founder claimed Queens had the worst inspection problem 'because it recorded the most critical violations.' Manhattan actually has the most (18,487 vs 13,253). Queens does lead both fair metrics — but the four other boroughs cluster within 3% of each other, and Queens sits only 9% above that cluster.
charts.form_why: On the findings tab this chart answers whether the claim survives. Here it demonstrates two display traps at once. First, the founder's own chart — a bar of raw counts — was a population census wearing a problem's clothes: a raw count across groups of different sizes ranks the sizes. Second, and more uncomfortable, THIS chart has its own failure mode: bump charts encode rank, and rank makes a hairline gap look like a landslide. A 2% difference and a 40% difference produce identical line crossings.
charts.method: Values print at every node specifically to defuse the rank illusion, and the caption is computed from the cluster shape rather than the global max-minus-min — so 'Queens is rank 1' and 'the lead is modest' cannot contradict each other on the same image. An earlier draft used a global spread statistic and produced exactly that contradiction.
charts.caution: Correcting a distortion can introduce its opposite. The founder's raw count exaggerated Queens's problem; a rank-only chart would have exaggerated its refutation. Neither denominator here is automatically fairer either — per-inspection reflects enforcement policy, per-restaurant confounds exposure time. The denominator has to follow the decision being made.

charts.title: The wrong form: a map for a pattern that isn't spatial
charts.insight: A stakeholder requested a map titled 'Where frequent inspections cause worse outcomes.' The association turned out to be 98% non-geographic — pooled slope +5.75, zip-demeaned slope +5.64 — so neighborhoods explain about 2% of it. The requested map would have shown a 'where' for something that has no where.
charts.form: Residual scatter map — a deliberate demotion
charts.form_why: Maps are persuasive because every dot is real, and that persuasiveness is exactly the risk: a map can show WHERE things coincide but never WHY, and this claim was entirely a why-claim. Rather than refuse the map, it was demoted to the one job a map can honestly do here — display what geography still explains AFTER cuisine and neighborhood means are removed. It renders as salt-and-pepper with no clusters, and that emptiness is the answer.
charts.method: Severity minus cuisine mean minus neighborhood mean, plotted per restaurant. 20,092 restaurants; 313 excluded for missing or (0,0) coordinates and counted rather than silently dropped. Aspect ratio set to roughly cos(latitude) so New York is not stretched — an unconsidered aspect ratio is itself a distortion.
charts.caution: The requested title contained the word 'cause' before any analysis had earned it — and in this domain the arrow runs backward, since risk-based enforcement assigns more inspections to worse restaurants. A title that names its conclusion in advance turns the chart into an illustration of a decision already made.

charts.title: Axis order is a causal claim — even when the title says otherwise
charts.insight: Restaurants scoring in the A range (0–13) receive 1.04 inspections on average; those scoring 41+ receive 2.18. The jump begins right at 14, which is where DOHMH's re-inspection rule fires. Scoring worse gets you inspected more.
charts.form: Bucketed line, cause on x and effect on y
charts.form_why: Readers parse x → y as cause → effect in the first two seconds, before any title is read. The Inspections tab's facet chart plots inspections on x and score on y, so its LAYOUT argues 'inspections make restaurants worse' — the reverse of the measured mechanism. Rewriting that chart's title fixed the words; this chart fixes the grammar. Same data, same window, same grain: only the axis assignment changed.
charts.method: One point per restaurant — its worst score and how many inspections it received — bucketed into DOHMH's own grading bands rather than invented cut points. n printed at every point. Zero baseline, deliberately: an earlier render started the y-axis at 1.0 and let a 1.04→2.18 climb fill the whole panel, which is the y-zoom lever two charts above this one.
charts.caution: Swapping axes does NOT establish causality. It aligns the visual grammar with a mechanism already known from the written enforcement rule. Absent that rule, this chart would imply the reverse just as readily — the honesty comes from the documented policy, not from the axis order.

cannot_answer: Whether any particular published chart was spun deliberately. These four levers are also the everyday choices of honest charting; intent is not visible in the output, which is precisely why disclosure matters more than motive.
Whether a chart is trustworthy from the chart alone. Two of these levers — the window search and the asymmetric smoothing — leave no visual trace at all. You need the method, not just the image.

How to make an unambiguously neutral chart, because there isn't one. Every chart chooses a window, a baseline, an aspect ratio, a smoothing policy, a color assignment and a caption. The honest ones disclose those choices; they do not avoid making them.
Whether these five exhaust the ways a chart misleads. They do not — they are the ones encountered while building this site, including two the author introduced and had to fix.
reproduce: python3 data/socrata/viz_borough_trend.py — writes honest.png, misleading.png and comparison.png in a single run · python3 data/socrata/export_scrolly.py — writes the series JSON the scroll piece renders from
